topics: Pediatric VA-ECMO, CPB vasoplegia and circuit safety
summaryHtml: This week's signal: five newly published papers met the date and relevance criteria. The strongest clinical signal came from pediatric medical VA-ECMO/ECPR risk stratification, while a CPB vasoplegia cohort, a methylene-blue circuit artifact case, an artificial-lung testing platform, and a VV-ECMO prone-positioning series added practical safety lessons. No new large randomized trial was identified that should immediately change CPB or ECMO protocols.

entries.title: Pediatric medical VA-ECMO: pre-ECMO physiology carried more prognostic information than ECPR status alone
entries.html:
Pediatric VA-ECMO · ECPRRetrospective cohortASAIO JournalNovember 18
Priority: TopClinical usefulness: 4.7/5

Pediatric medical VA-ECMO: pre-ECMO physiology carried more prognostic information than ECPR status alone

Study: Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation and Mortality in Pediatric Medical Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation.

Design: Single-center retrospective cohort of 73 children aged 28 days to <18 years receiving VA-ECMO for medical indications from 2010 to May 2025: non-ECPR n=58 and ECPR n=15.

Key findings

  • ECPR was associated with higher PICU mortality in unadjusted analysis (OR 5.23, 95% CI 1.47–18.53; P=0.010).
  • After adjustment for pre-ECMO physiologic variables, ECPR itself was no longer significantly associated with mortality (adjusted OR 1.74, 95% CI 0.37–8.08; P=0.483).
  • Lower pre-ECMO arterial pH remained associated with mortality: adjusted OR 1.87 for each 0.1-unit decrease (95% CI 1.20–2.92; P=0.006).
  • In sensitivity analysis, underlying cardiac disease was associated with lower mortality than noncardiac disease (adjusted OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.07–0.79).
Perfusionist briefing: Do not use “ECPR versus non-ECPR” as a stand-alone severity label. For pediatric VA-ECMO, the pre-cannulation physiologic state—especially the depth of acidosis—contains important prognostic information. At the bedside, interpret pH together with low-flow duration, lactate, perfusion pressure, organ dysfunction, underlying diagnosis, and the speed to effective ECMO flow. The pH signal is a risk marker, not an exclusion threshold.

Limitations: Single-center study with only 15 ECPR patients, wide confidence intervals after adjustment, and substantial potential for residual confounding. The findings should not be used to define a pediatric ECPR futility cutoff.

Read the PubMed record (PMID 43049872) →

entries.title: Preoperative ACEI/ARB use was not associated with post-CPB vasoplegia; ARNI showed a small-sample signal
entries.html:
CPB · VasoplegiaProspective observational cohortJ Surg ResNovember 18
Priority: HighClinical usefulness: 4.2/5

Preoperative ACEI/ARB use was not associated with post-CPB vasoplegia; ARNI showed a small-sample signal

Study: Preoperative RAAS Blockade Does Not Associate With Vasoplegia After Cardiopulmonary Bypass.

Design: Prospective observational cohort of 66 elective CPB patients at a tertiary referral center; 49 were classified as nonvasoplegic and 17 as vasoplegic using immediate postoperative vasopressor requirements and cardiac index.

Key findings

  • Preoperative beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor, ARB, statin, or combinations of these medications were not significantly associated with vasoplegia status.
  • All three patients taking an ARB-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) developed vasoplegia (3/17 vasoplegic vs 0/49 nonvasoplegic; P=0.015).
  • The authors concluded that post-CPB vasoplegia may involve pathways distinct from routine preoperative RAAS-modifying medication exposure.
Perfusionist briefing: Medication history remains part of the CPB weaning picture, but ACEI or ARB exposure alone should not be treated as a reliable predictor of vasoplegia. When SVR is low despite adequate flow and cardiac index, evaluate the full phenotype: temperature, acid-base status, calcium, vasopressor requirement, cardiac function, inflammatory burden, and preoperative medication history. The ARNI finding is worth noting, but it is far too small to justify a medication-withholding protocol change on its own.

Limitations: Only 66 patients were studied and only three were taking an ARNI. Medication discontinuation timing and other perioperative confounders may influence the results. This study cannot establish causality or define a preventive vasoplegia strategy.

Read the PubMed record (PMID 43051000) →

entries.title: Methylene blue can stain flexible PVC tubing and mimic membrane-lung failure
entries.html:
VA-ECMO · Membrane lungCase reportPerfusionNovember 17
Priority: HighClinical usefulness: 4.1/5

Methylene blue can stain flexible PVC tubing and mimic membrane-lung failure

Study: Apparent membrane lung dysfunction during veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation following methylene blue administration: Case report.

Design: Single case of a 72-year-old patient on central VA-ECMO for refractory cardiogenic and vasoplegic shock after cardiac surgery, with repeated methylene-blue boluses and infusions.

Key findings

  • After repeated methylene-blue administration, the post-membrane-lung flexible return tubing appeared dark, visually resembling poorly oxygenated blood.
  • Post-membrane-lung blood gases confirmed adequate oxygen exchange.
  • Blood appeared bright red within the membrane lung and rigid connectors; the apparent abnormality was caused by methylene-blue staining of the flexible PVC tubing rather than true membrane-lung dysfunction.
Perfusionist briefing: If the post-oxygenator side suddenly looks dark after methylene blue, do not diagnose oxygenator failure from tubing color alone. Confirm post-oxygenator PaO₂ and the pre/post gas-exchange pattern, review FdO₂ and sweep settings, and visually compare flexible tubing with rigid connectors or the oxygenator housing. If objective gas-exchange or pressure data show true failure, follow the normal membrane-lung exchange pathway.

Limitations: A single case cannot establish how often this artifact occurs or which tubing materials and methylene-blue doses are most susceptible. The lesson is diagnostic caution, not a new monitoring threshold.

Read the PubMed record (PMID 43043809) →

entries.title: Automated blood conditioning may make artificial-lung and oxygenator testing more reproducible
entries.html:
Artificial lung · Bench testingFeasibility studyASAIO JournalNovember 18
Priority: ModerateClinical usefulness: 3.9/5

Automated blood conditioning may make artificial-lung and oxygenator testing more reproducible

Study: Automated Blood Conditioning for Artificial Lung Evaluation: A Feasibility Study.

Design: In-vitro feasibility study of a closed-loop automated blood-conditioning platform using a hemoconcentrator, Terumo CDI 500, custom gas mixer, and PID controller. Four independent runs on separate blood batches totaled 48.5 hours.

Key findings

  • From arterial starting conditions, inlet oxygen saturation reached the venous target of 65% in about 5 minutes and pCO₂ reached 45 mmHg in about 6 minutes.
  • During steady state, 99.2% of oxygen-saturation measurements stayed within ±5% of target, with a reported error of 1.2%.
  • The primary run maintained physiologic conditions for its first 10 closed-loop hours.
  • The system tested device flows up to 0.6 L/min using 1.1 L of blood.
Perfusionist briefing: The immediate value is in device evaluation rather than bedside care. Stable, reproducible inlet blood conditions can improve comparisons of artificial lungs, oxygenators, and circuit prototypes and may also support standardized mock-circuit education. It is particularly relevant when interpreting bench oxygen-transfer data, where inconsistent inlet saturation or CO₂ can otherwise confound device comparisons.

Limitations: Low-flow bench study with only four blood batches; it does not establish performance at adult ECMO flows or clinical durability. The platform itself still requires broader validation before it can serve as a standardized testing method.

Read the PubMed record (PMID 43050695) →

entries.title: Prone positioning during VV-ECMO highlighted pressure-injury and cannula-management risks
entries.html:
VV-ECMO · Prone positioningCase seriesEnferm IntensivaNovember 17
Priority: ModerateClinical usefulness: 3.5/5

Prone positioning during VV-ECMO highlighted pressure-injury and cannula-management risks

Study: Adverse events in patients receiving venovenous ECMO and in the prone position simultaneously: A series of six cases.

Design: Six-patient case series from a tertiary ICU; all patients received VV-ECMO and at least one prone-positioning session.

Key findings

  • The main recorded care risks involved infection, bleeding, and impaired skin integrity.
  • Facial skin lesions occurred in 83% of the six cases.
  • The authors proposed that a femorojugular VV-ECMO configuration may restrict cervical rotation and make alternating pressure points more difficult.
  • Suggested preventive measures included prophylactic dressings, safe head micromobilization, and systematic skin assessment.
Perfusionist briefing: Proning on VV-ECMO is a team maneuver, not only a respiratory intervention. Before and after turning, verify cannula fixation and depth, tubing tension, drainage stability, pump flow, inlet pressure or chattering, and any change in recirculation or oxygenation. Head-position limits imposed by a jugular return cannula should be built into the pressure-injury prevention plan.

Limitations: Only six cases, so the 83% facial-injury figure should not be treated as a general incidence estimate. The study cannot prove that femorojugular cannulation caused the skin injuries.

Read the PubMed record (PMID 43044255) →

topics: VA-ECMO watershed physiology and circuit coatings
summaryHtml: This week's evidence check: the November 15 briefing did not identify a newly first-published CPB or ECMO paper within November 9–15. Instead of presenting older publications as new, this issue revisits two previously published studies with direct relevance to perfusion safety and circuit management. Their original online dates are shown on each card.

entries.title: VA-ECMO watershed physiology: cannulation configuration matters more than simply increasing flow
entries.html:
VA-ECMO · Differential hypoxemiaScoping reviewRev Cardiovasc MedFirst published September 30 · Revisited
Priority: HighClinical usefulness: 4.4/5

VA-ECMO watershed physiology: cannulation configuration matters more than simply increasing flow

Study: The Aortic Watershed Phenomenon and Differential Hypoxemia During Peripheral Venoarterial ECMO: A Scoping Review of Clinical and Experimental Evidence.

Design: PRISMA-ScR scoping review of clinical and experimental literature searched in MEDLINE and EMBASE. Of 245 records identified, 16 studies were included. First published online September 30, 2026 (DOI: 10.31083/RCM52934).

Key findings

  • Reported differential hypoxemia frequency ranged from 1.5% to 13.3% across included studies. This is a heterogeneous range, not a reliable pooled incidence estimate.
  • When native cardiac output recovers while pulmonary oxygenation remains poor, the aortic mixing interface may shift distally. Hypoxemic native blood can then supply the coronary and supra-aortic arteries even if femoral arterial oxygenation looks adequate.
  • Configuration-targeted approaches reported improvements in upper-body oxygenation or perfusion surrogates: move venous drainage toward the SVC/upper right atrium, convert to VAV-ECMO with controlled flow splitting and internal-jugular oxygenated return, or move arterial return toward a more proximal/antegrade site.
  • Beyond comparing upper- and lower-body oximetry and blood gases, the included literature described contrast-enhanced ultrasound, Doppler assessment, and positional CT angiography to examine mixing. Experimental models also showed why higher ECMO flow alone may not resolve the problem as native output increases.
Perfusionist briefing: In femoral VA-ECMO, assess right-hand saturation/right-radial arterial blood gases together with lower-body and circuit oxygenation, native ejection, and pulmonary status. A normal post-oxygenator or femoral gas does not exclude cerebral or myocardial hypoxemia. If differential hypoxemia develops, identify the underlying mixing and drainage problem before treating RPM escalation as the only solution. SVC-oriented drainage, VAV conversion, and antegrade return are configuration options requiring individualized cannula and flow assessment—not interchangeable bedside fixes.

Limitations: The 16 included studies used different definitions, detection thresholds, designs, and populations. Evidence for configuration changes is mainly physiological or based on small clinical series; the review does not prove that any one strategy improves survival or neurologic outcomes. Right-radial sampling is an important upper-body monitor but cannot directly establish coronary oxygenation.

Read the PubMed record (PMID 42985492) →

entries.title: Polymer-coated circuits showed lower lactate in vitro—but this is not evidence of better clinical perfusion
entries.html:
CPB circuit · Surface coatingIn-vitro comparative studyAsian Cardiovasc Thorac AnnFirst published September 2 · Revisited
Priority: ModerateClinical usefulness: 2.9/5

Polymer-coated circuits showed lower lactate in vitro—but this is not evidence of better clinical perfusion

Study: Hemocompatible polymer coating for extracorporeal circulation circuit affects lactate levels during cardiopulmonary bypass surgery.

Design: Small human whole-blood in-vitro comparison of polymer-coated (PC), heparin-coated (HC), and noncoated (NC) membrane-oxygenator circuits (reported n=5). Heparin diluted in a glucose solution was continuously administered; lactate, glucose, oxygen partial pressure, and oxygen saturation were measured at 0, 1, 3, 6, 12, and 24 hours. First published online September 2, 2026 (DOI: 10.1177/02184923261485742).

Key findings

  • Mean lactate was significantly lower in PC circuits than in HC and NC circuits at the sampled time points; HC and NC did not differ significantly in lactate.
  • Mean glucose was lower in NC circuits than in PC or HC circuits; PC and HC did not differ significantly in glucose.
  • Oxygen partial pressure and oxygen saturation did not differ significantly among the coating groups.
  • The abstract does not provide absolute lactate differences or patient outcomes, so the size and bedside relevance of the effect cannot be established from these results.
Perfusionist briefing: Circuit surface treatment may affect measured metabolic markers under controlled circulation conditions, independent of the oxygenation measures reported here. During clinical CPB, however, a rising lactate must still be evaluated with indexed oxygen delivery, pump flow, hemoglobin, perfusion pressure, temperature, glucose administration, and the patient's condition. These bench data do not justify choosing a coating based on lactate alone or interpreting lactate reduction as proven tissue-perfusion benefit.

Limitations: This was a small bench experiment, not a randomized clinical CPB study. Prolonged experimental circulation, glucose-containing heparin infusion, and the absence of patient-level endpoints limit clinical generalizability. The mechanisms of lower lactate and glucose remain uncertain; hemocompatibility as the cause was not directly established.

Read the PubMed record (PMID 42684926) →

summaryHtml: This week's signal: one newly published study met our relevance and date criteria. Rather than padding the list with older papers that only appeared in a November issue, this briefing focuses on the strongest new clinical signal: criteria-based ECMO use during lung transplantation and early neurologic complications.

entries.title: Criteria-based ECMO during lung transplantation was associated with fewer ischemic strokes
entries.html:
Lung transplant · ECMO/CPBRetrospective cohortTransplantationNovember 2
Priority: HighClinical usefulness: 4.2/5

Criteria-based ECMO during lung transplantation was associated with fewer ischemic strokes

Study: Incidence and Risk Factors for Early Major Neurologic Complications in Lung Transplantation: From Restrictive Cardiopulmonary Bypass to ECMO by Criteria.

Design: Single-center retrospective cohort of 389 lung transplant recipients, comparing an earlier restrictive-CPB era (2012–2017; n=288) with a later criteria-based ECMO era (2022–2024; n=101).

Key findings

  • Early major neurologic complications occurred in 10% versus 5% of patients; the difference in the proportion of affected patients was not statistically significant (P=0.152).
  • Total neurologic events were substantially more frequent in the earlier cohort (78 vs 8 events; incidence rate ratio 3.5, 95% CI 1.7–7.4).
  • Ischemic stroke was lower with criteria-based ECMO use: 2% versus 9% (P=0.022).
  • Intraoperative mechanical circulatory support was used more often in the ECMO-era cohort (43% vs 20%).
  • The apparent neurologic benefit came with trade-offs: greater intraoperative blood loss (2489 vs 1861 mL) and more severe primary graft dysfunction at 24 and 72 hours.
Perfusionist briefing: This does not mean ECMO should routinely replace CPB for every lung transplant. The useful signal is that a predefined, criteria-based support strategy may reduce exposure to unstable hypoxemia and cerebral hypoperfusion while avoiding CPB when it is not required. If ECMO is chosen, cerebral oxygenation, upper-body gas exchange, cannula position and flow, anticoagulation, blood loss, and graft reperfusion all remain part of the same safety problem.

Limitations: The two groups came from different eras, so surgical technique, donor/recipient selection, ICU care, transfusion practice, and ECMO experience may all have changed. The later cohort was also older and had more cardiopulmonary comorbidity. This is hypothesis-generating evidence, not proof that ECMO itself caused the lower stroke rate.

Read the PubMed record (PMID 42968367) →

topics: VA-ECMO unloading, ECPR lactate and outcomes
summaryHtml: Week in review: the strongest perfusion signal was mechanistic rather than outcome-changing. HERACLES directly compared IABP and a microaxial flow pump during VA-ECMO, while the ECPR studies reinforced that post-reperfusion physiology and center-level systems matter. None of these studies establishes a new device-selection or prognostication threshold.

entries.title: HERACLES: IABP improved myocardial oxygen supply–demand balance during VA-ECMO
entries.html:
VA-ECMO · LV unloadingRandomized mechanistic trialCirc Cardiovasc IntervOctober 31
Priority: HighClinical usefulness: 4.5/5

HERACLES: IABP improved myocardial oxygen supply–demand balance during VA-ECMO

Study: Hemodynamic Effects of Reducing LV Afterload With Impella or Intra-Aortic Balloon Counterpulsation During Veno-Arterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation in Cardiogenic Shock: HERACLES Trial.

Design: Randomized mechanistic trial of 24 patients with cardiogenic shock on VA-ECMO, comparing IABP with a microaxial flow pump. Most patients were SCAI stage D/E; median LVEF was 10%.

Key findings

  • The myocardial oxygen supply–demand ratio improved with IABP but not with the microaxial pump: 1.48 versus 0.97 (P=0.036).
  • The difference was driven mainly by reduced LV systolic pressure-time integral; both devices reduced LV pressures.
  • Coronary flow increased marginally with IABP and was unchanged with the microaxial pump.
  • Thirty-day mortality was similar (38% vs 45%; P=0.84); the trial was not designed to prove a survival difference.
Perfusionist briefing: “LV unloading” is not a single physiological effect. Two devices can both lower LV pressure while producing different coronary-flow and myocardial oxygen-balance responses. For VA-ECMO patients, device choice should still be tied to the actual problem—LV distension, pulmonary edema, absent aortic opening, myocardial recovery, or systemic perfusion—not to this small surrogate-endpoint trial alone.

Limitations: Only 24 patients were randomized. The primary endpoint was mechanistic, not mortality or recovery, and invasive measurements were made under controlled study conditions. The findings do not establish clinical superiority of IABP over a microaxial pump.

Read the PubMed record (PMID 42966011) →

entries.title: After ECPR, the 12-hour lactate response carried more information than the prereperfusion value
entries.html:
ECPR · ReperfusionRetrospective cohortASAIO JournalOctober 29
Priority: HighClinical usefulness: 4.2/5

After ECPR, the 12-hour lactate response carried more information than the prereperfusion value

Study: Dynamic Early Postreperfusion Physiology Is Associated With Organ Recovery After Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation.

Design: Retrospective study of 91 patients with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest treated with ECPR; paired prereperfusion and 12-hour lactate values were available in 38 patients.

Key findings

  • Twelve-hour lactate was lower in survivors than nonsurvivors (5.45 vs 9.04 mmol/L; P=0.002), while prereperfusion lactate did not differ.
  • In paired data, mortality discrimination increased from AUC 0.47 before reperfusion to 0.80 at 12 hours.
  • Each 5 mmol/L higher 12-hour lactate was associated with higher mortality (OR 2.73), lower odds of ECMO weaning (OR 0.44), and more cerebral edema/hypoxic injury (OR 2.07) after adjustment for low-flow duration.
Perfusionist briefing: The useful message is the trajectory, not a single lactate cutoff. After ECPR, falling lactate should be interpreted alongside ECMO flow, native pulsatility, MAP, Hb, gas exchange, vasopressor dose, urine output, and regional perfusion. A persistently high lactate at 12 hours should prompt reassessment of unresolved shock or ischemia, but it is not a stand-alone futility rule.

Limitations: Small retrospective cohort, only 38 paired measurements, and strong potential for confounding by shock severity and treatment response. The study identifies associations and does not validate a treatment threshold.

Read the PubMed record (PMID 42956360) →

entries.title: ECMO in infarction-related cardiogenic shock: large dataset, but no valid causal comparison
entries.html:
MI cardiogenic shock · ECMONational observational cohortJ Am Heart AssocOctober 30
Priority: Moderate–HighClinical usefulness: 4.0/5

ECMO in infarction-related cardiogenic shock: large dataset, but no valid causal comparison

Study: National Use Patterns and Comparative Effectiveness of Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation in Myocardial Infarction-Related Cardiogenic Shock.

Design: Medicare-based retrospective cohort of 102,718 patients with MI-related cardiogenic shock from 2016–2023: ECMO 1,165, Impella 10,064, IABP 24,631, and medical management 66,858.

Key findings

  • ECMO use increased from 0.8% to 1.8%, while the proportion of hospitals using ECMO rose from 9.2% to 17.1%.
  • Unadjusted 30-day mortality was 69% with ECMO, 60% with Impella, 39% with IABP, and 46% with medical therapy.
  • IPTW and G-formula analyses still estimated ECMO mortality at 68–70%, but a grace-period analysis yielded 54% mortality for both ECMO and Impella.
  • The authors explicitly concluded that valid causal inference about ECMO and survival could not be established.
Perfusionist briefing: Do not interpret the crude mortality table as “ECMO is worse.” VA-ECMO is commonly deployed later and in more profound shock. The study is more useful as a reminder that cannulation timing, arrest status, shock stage, and prior MCS must be captured when comparing outcomes across programs.

Limitations: Administrative Medicare data, an older population, residual confounding by indication, and no detailed information on ECMO flow, cannulation, LV unloading, lactate, or shock phenotype.

Read the PubMed record (PMID 42960751) →

entries.title: Pediatric ECPR outcomes still varied between centers after risk adjustment
entries.html:
Pediatric ECPRELSO registryCritical Care MedicineOctober 29
Priority: Moderate–HighClinical usefulness: 3.9/5

Pediatric ECPR outcomes still varied between centers after risk adjustment

Study: Variation in Pediatric Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Survival After In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: Development and Validation of a Survival Model for Risk-Standardized Survival Rates.

Design: ELSO Registry multicenter cohort of 1,377 children with in-hospital cardiac arrest treated with ECPR (2020–2023); derivation n=1,060 and internal validation n=317.

Key findings

  • The 14-variable model had AUC 0.728 in derivation and 0.678 in validation, with good internal calibration.
  • After patient-level risk adjustment, between-hospital variation remained significant; median odds ratio was 1.30 (95% CI 1.11–1.93).
  • The authors cautioned that discrimination is not strong enough for the model to be used as a stand-alone bedside decision tool.
Perfusionist briefing: This is a systems paper as much as a prognostication paper. Differences in ECPR activation, cannulation readiness, low-flow time, team training, and post-cannulation management may contribute to center-level variation. It supports auditing ECPR processes, not using a score to deny an individual child support.

Limitations: Internal validation only, registry-variable constraints, possible residual differences in case mix and center practice, and only fair discrimination for individual prediction.

Read the PubMed record (PMID 42951894) →

entries.title: Stellate ganglion block did not prevent postoperative atrial fibrillation after valve surgery
entries.html:
Cardiac surgery · CPBRandomized double-blind trialJ Am Heart AssocOctober 30
Priority: LowClinical usefulness: 3.0/5

Stellate ganglion block did not prevent postoperative atrial fibrillation after valve surgery

Study: Efficacy of Stellate Ganglion Block for Preventing Postoperative Atrial Fibrillation After Cardiac Surgery: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial.

Design: Single-center randomized double-blind trial of 140 valve-surgery patients undergoing CPB; 132 were included in the modified intention-to-treat analysis.

Key findings

  • POAF occurred in 43% after stellate ganglion block versus 40% with saline (adjusted P=0.989): the primary endpoint was negative.
  • Secondary signals favored SGB for VF/VT requiring defibrillation after cross-clamp release (6% vs 19%), postoperative hs-troponin I, and AKI (5% vs 18%).
Perfusionist briefing: The defibrillation-after-unclamping signal is interesting for the operating room, but this is not a perfusion intervention and should not change current CPB practice. It is best viewed as a hypothesis about autonomic modulation and reperfusion arrhythmias.

Limitations: Single-center trial, negative primary endpoint, and the favorable arrhythmia, troponin, and AKI findings were secondary outcomes that require replication.

Read the PubMed record (PMID 42960736) →

topics: ECPR timing, aortic surgery and ECMO cannulation
summaryHtml: Week in review: two studies were especially relevant to perfusion systems: a nationwide target-trial emulation of ECPR timing and a temperature-strategy study in emergency aortic surgery. Both support physiology- and system-aware decision making, but neither supplies a new hard cutoff for cannulation time or hypothermia temperature.

entries.title: Earlier ECPR was associated with the largest benefit, but 60 minutes was not an absolute futility boundary
entries.html:
ECPR · TimingTarget-trial emulationEHJ Acute Cardiovascular CareOctober 25
Priority: TopClinical usefulness: 4.7/5

Earlier ECPR was associated with the largest benefit, but 60 minutes was not an absolute futility boundary

Study: Earlier Versus Later Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation in Refractory Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Nationwide Sequential Landmark Target Trial Emulation.

Design: Korean nationwide OHCA registry study (2016–2023) using sequential landmark target-trial emulation. Among 58,668 refractory OHCA patients, 909 received ECPR.

Key findings

  • Weighted 30-day survival with ECPR versus continued conventional CPR was 31.0% vs 16.0% at the 15-minute landmark, 21.6% vs 7.2% at 30 minutes, and 10.9% vs 3.2% at 60 minutes.
  • Adjusted survival differences were +15.0, +14.4, and +7.7 percentage points, respectively (all P<0.001).
  • Favorable neurologic outcomes followed a similar pattern; exploratory benefit decreased with longer door-to-ECMO time but remained statistically significant through 120 minutes.
Perfusionist briefing: The operational message is “earlier is better,” not “late is useless.” For an ECPR program, the modifiable targets are recognition, team activation, cannulation readiness, and time to full flow. A patient crossing 60 minutes should not be rejected solely because of the clock if the rest of the candidacy profile remains favorable.

Limitations: Observational data despite sophisticated target-trial methods, residual confounding and selection remain possible, and the cohort was restricted to presumed cardiac-cause refractory OHCA. The results do not prove benefit for every late ECPR candidate.

Read the PubMed record (PMID 42926135) →

entries.title: Emergency hemiarch surgery: warmer hypothermia strategies showed a stroke signal, not a new temperature target
entries.html:
Aortic surgery · CPBRetrospective cohortPerfusionOctober 22
Priority: HighClinical usefulness: 4.4/5

Emergency hemiarch surgery: warmer hypothermia strategies showed a stroke signal, not a new temperature target

Study: Impact of hypothermia level on neurological and renal outcomes in emergency aortic surgery: a single-centre experience.

Design: Single-center retrospective cohort of 175 acute aortic syndrome operations (2018–2023); 89% underwent hemiarch replacement. Patients were grouped as ≤20°C, 20.1–24°C, 24.1–28°C, and >28°C.

Key findings

  • CPB duration fell progressively with warmer strategies, from a median 270.5 minutes in deep hypothermia to 164 minutes in mild hypothermia.
  • Overall 30-day mortality was 18.9% and stroke 19.4%.
  • In the hemiarch subgroup, stroke occurred in 27%, 26%, 8.8%, and 11% across the four temperature groups (P=0.049).
  • The four-category association was no longer significant after multivariable adjustment; a separate >24°C versus ≤24°C sensitivity analysis was associated with lower stroke risk (OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.08–0.64).
  • No clear AKI advantage was demonstrated across temperature groups.
Perfusionist briefing: This supports the direction of modern hemiarch practice—avoiding unnecessarily deep cooling when an appropriate cerebral-protection strategy is used—but it does not establish “24°C” as a universal target. Procedure extent, ACP strategy, arrest time, rewarming, embolic risk, and institutional experience still determine the temperature plan.

Limitations: Retrospective, single center, major coupling between temperature, cerebral-perfusion strategy, CPB duration, procedure complexity, and era. The mild-hypothermia group was small, and results for total arch replacement remain uncertain.

Read the PubMed record (PMID 42911832) →

entries.title: Cerebral microbleed burden tracked with extracorporeal-circulation exposure
entries.html:
CPB · Neurologic safetyRetrospective MRI studyJ Cereb Blood Flow MetabOctober 20
Priority: Moderate–HighClinical usefulness: 3.8/5

Cerebral microbleed burden tracked with extracorporeal-circulation exposure

Study: Cerebral microbleed burden after aortic and cardiac surgery is associated with extracorporeal circulation exposure: Evidence from young patients with heritable connective tissue disorders.

Design: Retrospective brain-MRI study of 111 genetically confirmed patients with heritable connective tissue disorders, relating cerebral microbleeds to surgical and extracorporeal-circulation exposure.

Key findings

  • All 58 patients exposed to surgery using extracorporeal circulation had cerebral microbleeds, compared with 4 of 53 surgery-naïve patients.
  • Microbleeds were predominantly lobar.
  • Burden increased with repeated procedures and, when duration data were available, with longer extracorporeal-circulation exposure (P<0.001).
  • Valve type and surgical technique were not associated with microbleed burden.
Perfusionist briefing: This is a strong imaging signal that neurologic injury after extracorporeal circulation may be cumulative and multifactorial. It reinforces meticulous de-airing, minimizing avoidable circuit exposure and suction-related air/blood interfaces, and attention to embolic and perfusion safety—but it does not identify a single responsible device or technique.

Limitations: Highly selected connective-tissue-disorder population, retrospective imaging, no direct measurement of intraoperative embolic load, and no demonstrated link between microbleed count and functional neurologic outcomes.

Read the PubMed record (PMID 42899414) →

entries.title: Axillary graft versus direct femoral arterial return after heart transplant: no proven superiority
entries.html:
Heart transplant · VA-ECMORetrospective cohortBiomedicinesOctober 21
Priority: ModerateClinical usefulness: 3.6/5

Axillary graft versus direct femoral arterial return after heart transplant: no proven superiority

Study: Axillary Dacron Graft Versus Direct Femoral Arterial Cannulation for Peripheral VA-ECMO After Heart Transplantation: A Single-Center Cohort Study.

Design: Retrospective single-center cohort of 42 heart-transplant recipients requiring peripheral VA-ECMO for primary graft dysfunction: axillary Dacron graft n=17 versus direct femoral arterial cannulation n=25.

Key findings

  • Cannulation-related complications occurred in 0/17 axillary cases and 3/25 femoral cases (12%); OR 0.18, 95% CI 0.01–3.80, P=0.260.
  • Successful weaning was similar: 94.1% versus 92.0%.
  • Survival to discharge was 76.5% versus 64.0% (P=0.505), and stroke 5.9% versus 16.0% (P=0.632).
  • None of the between-group differences reached statistical significance.
Perfusionist briefing: Axillary return offers antegrade systemic flow and avoids direct femoral return, but this small series cannot prove fewer vascular or neurologic complications. Cannulation choice should remain anatomy- and urgency-specific, with attention to achievable flow, limb/upper-extremity perfusion, graft hemostasis, and differential oxygenation.

Limitations: Very small single-center cohort, wide confidence intervals, nonrandom cannulation selection, and limited power for uncommon vascular or neurologic complications.

Read the PubMed record (PMID 42940214) →

entries.title: Age ≥50 years was associated with lower long-term graft survival after ECMO bridging
entries.html:
ECMO bridge · Lung transplantRetrospective cohortPneumologieOctober 21
Priority: ModerateClinical usefulness: 3.3/5

Age ≥50 years was associated with lower long-term graft survival after ECMO bridging

Study: Age-related Long-Term Outcomes after ECMO Bridging to Lung Transplantation: A 15-Year Single-Center Experience.

Design: Fifteen-year single-center retrospective cohort of 115 adults listed for lung transplantation while receiving ECMO; 93 underwent transplantation. Patients were prespecified as <50 versus ≥50 years.

Key findings

  • Post-transplant 1-, 3-, and 5-year graft survival was 87%, 83%, and 77% in recipients <50 years versus 72%, 53%, and 44% in those ≥50.
  • Age ≥50 was independently associated with graft loss (adjusted HR 2.53, 95% CI 1.14–5.59; P=0.022).
  • Among follow-up survivors, older recipients had more comorbidity, lower exercise capacity, and lower return-to-work rates, while marked frailty remained uncommon.
Perfusionist briefing: This is primarily a candidate-selection and recovery study, not an ECMO-management study. Age should not be treated as a stand-alone exclusion threshold; functional reserve, frailty, organ dysfunction, rehabilitation potential, and trajectory on ECMO remain more informative at the bedside.

Limitations: Single-center experience spanning 15 years of evolving ECMO and transplant practice, substantial selection before listing and transplantation, and limited generalizability to all ECMO bridge candidates.
